title: Ad giant reveals new AI road map
full_text:
Australian businesses are fast approaching an AI adoption tipping point as the market begins to connect data, technology and creative capabilities to create measurable commercial outcomes, according to WPP’s Australian leadership.
The prediction comes as the holding company bets on its new structure, which compromises creative, media, production and technology capabilities that are integrated by its AI system, WPP Open, which will help brands unlock new customers and extract greater returns from their marketing investments.
WPP ANZ chief executive Rose Herceg said the integrated model was increasingly helping to identify and unlock new opportunities and avenues for product development and growth for clients. “There are more examples now where by using WPP Open, we are now seeing a brand new audience that our client would never have considered,” Ms Herceg said.
Most significantly, this is helping to accelerate the shift in client conversations, from questions about efficiency to a broader understanding of what AI could deliver across their businesses.
Ms Herceg said one client had identified an additional audience of several million Australians it had not previously considered commercially accessible, creating opportunities to reach new customers, adapt products and deliver growth. “That opens up opportunities. It opens up an audience, it opens up conversations about new product development, how we can tweak the product we have for that audience,” she said.
“It makes the CFO of the company really happy, because all of a sudden, they’re getting their 3-5 per cent growth.” Her comments come as advertising groups face mounting pressure to demonstrate the commercial value of AI investments, with businesses increasingly looking beyond productivity gains and automation to understand how the technology can translate into stronger customer relationships and revenue. WPP Production ANZ managing director Dan Robathan said the industry needed to move beyond the prevailing mandate to use AI to reduce costs.
“The conversation that we want to be having is, ‘I’ve worked out how to save you 10 per cent’. The conversation we’re having is ‘I’ve worked out how to use these tools in our relationships to 2X, 3X, 4X our business’,” he said.
“The mandate was ‘we need to use this to save money’. The tipping point is ‘we can work with the right partner to truly affect tangible growth’.” However, trust remains the biggest barrier to unlocking growth opportunities, with businesses requiring greater confidence that the technology will improve the quality and effectiveness of their communications, rather than simply generate more content at a lower cost.
And as AI adoption matures at different speeds across the industry, businesses are increasingly grappling with the complexity of their existing technology investments and proliferating AI tools.
WPP Enterprise ANZ president Tim Matheson said “a lot more technical support” was needed.
He said that, while clients were experimenting with a growing range of tools, they were struggling to integrate them into end-to-end processes.
“There are so many tools. This is moving so fast,” he said. “There is definitely an expectation of a lot more for a lot less. And the quality of that is questionable.” With the growing importance of first-party data, loyalty programs and direct customer relationships, there is also significant demand for more sophisticated marketing infrastructure. Brands are increasingly requiring systems that can create and maintain relevant and consistent relationships with customers who are moving between marketplaces, social commerce and other channels.
“The thirst for more and more content is there,” Mr Matheson said. “The risk is it’s poorly timed and crap. So getting it right is harder than ever.” The opportunity for brands continues to lie within the integration of all the different elements to deliver one continuous relationship between brands and consumers. This meant abandoning the outdated idea that customer journeys were a linear process, Mr Robathan said.
“The biggest challenge is making sure [the relationship] never ends,” he said. “If we’re doing it properly, it never ends because you’re not relieved when someone bought something because you stop hearing from someone. You’re vested in that conversation and the communication becomes a point of value rather than, at best, a useful distraction. It’s a moment of joy.” This is where WPP argues its simplified structure comes into great effect, as it can combine its expertise across data, technology, media, creative and production to create these relevant communications that can build those relationships between brands and consumers.
However, Ms Herceg said the focus must shift from functional benefits to tap into the more emotional connection that would appeal to consumers. “It’s very easy to go to what is utilitarian in a tricky economy and it’s so easy to forget, to entertain and inform your customer base in a way that makes them feel good about themselves or the world or their product and their brand,” Ms Herceg said. She said consumer research continued to show a desire for originality, inspiration and joy, creating an opportunity for brands to differentiate themselves via more meaningful communications: “No AI can make me feel that humanity. But we can make the AI give us joy through the production of what we do.”
